rows: Odd index: this element must be ≥ its left neighbour

blocks.h: Why does a swap not break the earlier pair?
p: Suppose pair (i−1, i−2) already satisfies its relation and we swap positions i−1 and i because of a violation. For an odd i, nums[i] < nums[i−1] and the pair before required nums[i−2] ≥ nums[i−1]; after the swap the new nums[i−1] is the smaller of the two, so nums[i−2] ≥ it still holds. The even case is symmetric. One left-to-right pass is therefore enough.

280.takeaway: Wiggle sort in one pass: fix each adjacent pair by swapping when the up/down relation is violated; the swap keeps the earlier relation true.

p: Tree `[1,null,3,2,4,null,null,null,5]` (3 has children 2 and 4; 4 has right child 5). Answer: 3 (3 → 4 → 5).

blocks.h: Why pass the run downward instead of returning it?
p: The sequence must go downwards from parent to child, so each node only needs its parent's value and run length. A top-down DFS (Depth-First Search) carries these as arguments, and no combining of children's results is needed.

298.takeaway: Top-down DFS (Depth-First Search): pass the parent value and current run length; extend the run when value = parent + 1, else restart.

blocks.h: Why mark first and wrap later?
p: Matches may overlap (`aaa` and `aab` share letters) or touch (`aab` ends where `bc` starts). If tags were inserted per match you would need to merge them afterwards. With one flag per character, a bold run is simply a maximal stretch of True flags, so merging is automatic: in the second example every character except the last `c` is covered, giving one tag pair.

bullets: Time: O(n·w·L) in the worst case for searching; marking and output are O(n).

616.takeaway: Mark every covered character first, then open a tag at the start of each run of flags and close it at the end.

Bit i set means target[i] is covered
One entry for each subset of target positions
`first = next((i for … if not (mask >> i) & 1), None)`
Every solution must cover this letter with some sticker, so only stickers containing it need to be tried
A sticker can be used for repeated letters at most as often as they appear on it

p: Target `thehat` (positions 0–5), stickers `with example science`. Bits are written left to right, one per target letter (1 = covered). The cheapest chain found by the DP uses 3 stickers:

blocks.h: Why always fix the first uncovered letter?
p: Without this rule the same set of stickers could be applied in many orders, creating redundant states. Insisting that the next sticker covers the first missing letter orders the choices canonically and cuts the transitions per state to the stickers containing that letter. Impossible targets leave `dp[-1] = INF` and the function returns −1.

bullets: Time: O(2ⁿ · s · n) with s stickers.

691.takeaway: Bitmask DP over covered letters: from each state, apply a sticker that covers the first missing letter and take the minimum count.

blocks.h: Why group the same answers together?
p: To minimise the total, assume rabbits giving the same answer share colours as much as possible. Two rabbits saying 1 can be the same colour pair (group of 2). One rabbit saying 2 needs a group of 3 even though the other two never answered. A third rabbit saying 1 would need a second group of 2.

781.takeaway: Group equal answers: c rabbits saying a need ceil(c/(a+1)) groups of size a+1.

p: Each character multiplies the number of strings by 2 (letters) or 1 (digits). The list `res` always contains all strings for the prefix processed so far, so no recursion or undo is needed (compare backtracking on a shared list).

What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Cheapest known price to each city using at most r flights
k stops = k+1 flights = k+1 rounds
Each round allows one more flight
Relaxations in this round must read only the previous round's values
Is flying u→v cheaper than the best known for v?
Moves from r flights to r+1 flights

p: 4 cities, `src = 0`, `dst = 3`, `k = 1` (so at most 2 flights):

blocks.h: Why copy the array each round?
p: Without `nxt`, a single round could chain several flights (0→1 then 1→2 in the same pass), ignoring the limit on stops. Reading from `dist` and writing to `nxt` ensures that after round r every value uses at most r flights. Here that gives 700 for city 3; the cheaper 0→1→2→3 (400) needs three flights and is excluded with k = 1.

Dijkstra picks the globally cheapest path, but a cheap path with too many stops is invalid and an expensive path with fewer stops may be needed. Bellman-Ford with a round limit keeps the number of flights as part of the state.

787.takeaway: Bellman-Ford limited to k+1 rounds: relax all flights from a snapshot of the previous round so each round adds exactly one flight.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `dp[i]` = ways to tile a 2 × i board; `dp[0] = 1` (the empty board), `dp[1] = 1`, `dp[2] = 2`
Last and third-last items of the list
The previous values, without index arithmetic

p: Values from the recurrence compared with an exhaustive count of tilings (brute force over a bitmask of covered cells):

blocks.h: Where does the recurrence come from?
bullets: Let f(n) be the number of full tilings of 2×n and g(n) the number of tilings of a 'jagged' board (2×n with one extra cell sticking out in the next column).
A full tiling ends with a vertical domino (f(n−1)), two horizontal dominoes (f(n−2)), or one of two mirror-image trominoes completing a jagged board (2·g(n−1)): f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) + 2·g(n−1).
A jagged board either ends with a horizontal domino on the long side (g(n−1)) or a tromino-plus-fill (f(n−2)): g(n) = g(n−1) + f(n−2).
Subtracting f(n−1) from f(n) and substituting g(n−1) − g(n−2) = f(n−3) gives f(n) − f(n−1) = f(n−1) + f(n−3), i.e. f(n) = 2·f(n−1) + f(n−3).
Space: O(n) (could be O(1) keeping three values).

790.takeaway: Tiling recurrence f(n) = 2·f(n−1) + f(n−3), obtained by tracking full and jagged boards and eliminating the jagged ones.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Trailing zeros of x! = x//5 + x//25 + …
Count factors of 5 (see Factorial Trailing Zeroes)
Safe upper bound for the answer
f(5(k+1)) ≥ k+1 > k, so the first x with f(x) ≥ k is below it
f is non-decreasing in x, so we can find the first x with f(x) ≥ k
f only increases when x passes a multiple of 5, so if any x gives k, exactly the five x in a block of consecutive numbers do

p: `k = 5` returns 0: the search ends at lo = 25 with f(lo) = 6 ≠ 5 (f jumps from 4 at x = 24 to 6 at x = 25, skipping 5).
`k = 3` has x = 15…19 (five values); `k = 0` has x = 0…4 (five values).

blocks.h: Why is the answer only ever 0 or 5?
p: f(x) is constant on blocks 5m … 5m+4 and rises at each multiple of 5 (by one, or more at multiples of 25, which is why some k are skipped). So the set {x : f(x) = k} is empty or a full block of five.

bullets: Time: O(log² k): the binary search takes O(log k) steps and each `f` call is O(log k).

793.takeaway: Binary search for the first x whose trailing-zero count reaches k; the preimage has size 5 if it hits k exactly, else 0.

What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Otherwise `goal in s + s` could succeed for a shorter goal
Every rotation of s appears as a substring of s + s
Python's `in` on strings searches for a contiguous match

blocks.h: Why does the doubled string work?
p: Rotating s by k shifts its first k letters to the end. In `s + s` the substring starting at index k of length n is exactly that rotation. Conversely, any length-n substring of `s + s` starting at 0…n−1 is a rotation. The length check rules out partial matches.

bullets: Time: O(n) with a linear-time search (Python's `in` is typically fast but not guaranteed linear in the worst case).
Space: O(n) for the doubled string.

796.takeaway: A string is a rotation of another exactly when it appears inside the doubled string and has the same length.

bullets: Time: O(query_row²) — row r has r+1 glasses.

p: `[[1,2],[2,3],[5],[0],[5],[],[]]` → [2, 4, 5, 6]. Nodes 0, 1, 3 lie on or lead into the cycle 0→1→3→0 and are never freed:

This is topological sorting (Kahn's algorithm) on the reversed graph. Safety flows backwards: a node is safe if all its successors are safe. Starting from terminals and removing edges backwards finds exactly the nodes that cannot reach a cycle.

802.takeaway: Safe nodes = those that cannot reach a cycle: run Kahn's topological sort on the reversed graph starting from terminals.

p: `[1,null,0,0,1]` written as `value(left,right)` with `·` for none: before `1(·,0(0,1))`, after `1(·,0(·,1))`. Nodes are finished in this order:

p: `['time','me','bell']`: suffixes that are also words are discarded; survivors ['bell', 'time'] give 10 (`time#bell#`).

blocks.h: Why does discarding suffixes give the shortest encoding?
p: If a word is a suffix of another word, it can read off the tail of the longer word's encoding for free (start at the right index, stop at the `#`). Words that aren't suffixes of anything else must be written out. So the answer is the sum of (length + 1) over words that are not proper suffixes of other words.

bullets: Time: O(Σ L²): each word creates up to L suffixes of up to L characters.

820.takeaway: Remove every word that is a proper suffix of another word; the rest are written out once each with a trailing #.

Is the starting number a a whole positive integer?
Solve n = k·a + k(k−1)/2 for a

p: A run of k consecutive numbers starting at a sums to k·a + (0+1+…+(k−1)) = k·a + k(k−1)/2. For n = 15 and k = 3: 3a + 3 = 15 gives a = 4, so 4+5+6. The condition `k·a ≥ k` (a ≥ 1) is guaranteed by the loop bound `k(k+1)/2 ≤ n`. Since k grows as about √(2n), the loop is O(√n).

829.takeaway: Try every run length k: n = k·a + k(k−1)/2 has a positive integer start a exactly when n − k(k−1)/2 is divisible by k.

Simulates the editor without building the final string
Each `#` adds one; each normal character consumes one
Compare the two strings from the end
Backspaces affect characters to their LEFT, so scanning right-to-left sees them first
One string has a surviving letter and the other doesn't

p: `'ab#c'` and `'ad#c'` (both type `ac`):
Result False: the first surviving letters are `c` and `b`.

Reading left to right you cannot know whether a letter will be deleted until later backspaces arrive. From the right, a `#` is seen before the letters it deletes, so a simple counter decides survival. This avoids building two edited strings (the stack solution uses O(n) space; this uses O(1)).

844.takeaway: Compare from the right with a skip counter: backspaces are seen before the letters they delete, so no stack is needed.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Cars from closest to the target to furthest
A car can only be blocked by cars ahead of it
Time to reach the target if never blocked
This car would arrive later than the fleet ahead
It can't catch up, so it forms a new fleet
Arrival time of the newest (slowest) fleet
A car arriving earlier or at the same time merges into that fleet

p: `target = 12`, positions `[10,8,0,5,3]`, speeds `[2,4,1,1,3]`: 3 fleets.

Processing from the front, if the car behind would arrive no later than the fleet ahead, it catches up and then has to slow down to the fleet's pace (or arrives exactly together), so it joins that fleet. If it would arrive later, it never catches up. So the fleet count is the number of strict increases in arrival time while scanning from the front. (Equal times mean meeting at the target, which counts as one fleet.)

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for sorting.
Space: O(n) for the sorted list.

853.takeaway: Sort by position descending and count each car whose unobstructed arrival time exceeds every fleet ahead of it.
